fuente.nota: Text shortened by removing paragraphs; the sentences are unchanged.

parrafos: Water (H2O) is a simple chemical compound made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. It is clear, has no taste or smell, and is almost colorless. All living things need water to survive. Water molecules stick together because of hydrogen bonds. These bonds give water special properties. For example, water has high surface tension, and can dissolve many substances. Water exists in three forms on Earth: solid (ice), liquid (water), and gas (water vapor). The word "water" comes from the Old English word wæter.

Water has many unique abilities. One is that it expands when it freezes. This makes ice less dense than liquid water, so ice floats. Water also has a high specific heat capacity. It can absorb or lose a lot of heat without changing temperature much. This helps keep Earth's climate stable. Water’s surface tension lets it form droplets. It also lets small insects walk on water. Water is an excellent solvent. It can dissolve more substances than any other liquid. This is why it is called the "universal solvent." However, it cannot dissolve oily or nonpolar substances well. These special abilities come from water's polar nature and the hydrogen bonds between them.

Water is important for all living things. Every kind of life we know needs water to survive. This includes tiny living things like bacteria, archaea, and protists, and bigger ones like fungi, plants and animals. The human body is about 50-60% water. Water helps move nutrients, gases, and waste inside the body. Inside cells, water is where most chemical reactions happen. It also helps cells keep their shape. Water is needed for digestion in animals, and photosynthesis in plants. It also helps control body temperature. Without water, life could not exist. That is why water is one of the most important substances for all living things.

Water is also very important to the world economy. About 70% of the fresh water people use goes to farming. Water is used to grow crops and raise animals. Fish from oceans, lakes, and rivers are an important source of food. Many products, like crude oil and other goods, are moved around the world by ships through oceans, rivers, and canals. Water is also used to heat and cool buildings and machines. Because it can dissolve many substances, it is very useful in factories, cooking, and cleaning. Water can also be used to make electricity, using hydroelectric plants. It is also used for fun activities like swimming, boating, fishing, diving, ice skating, snowboarding, and skiing.

Many civilizations in history began near rivers or other places where they could get water easily. For example, Mesopotamia began between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Ancient Egypt depended on the Nile. The Indus Valley civilization started near the Indus River. Ancient Rome was built near the Tiber River. Even today, many big cities like London, New York, and Shanghai grew near water. Being close to rivers or oceans made it easier to trade and travel. Islands with good harbors, like Singapore, also became rich and powerful because ships could stop there easily. In dry places like North Africa and the Middle East, clean water has always been important. Having water often made the difference between a small village and a strong civilization.

Water is not just found on Earth. Scientists have discovered water in many places in space. Ice has been found on Mars, and even on the Moon. Some moons in our solar system, like Europa and Ganymede (around Jupiter), and Enceladus (around Saturn) may have liquid water under their icy surfaces. Water vapor has also been found in the atmosphere of some exoplanets. These are planets that orbit stars far away from our solar system. Water has even been found in clouds of gas and dust in space where new stars are being born.

Shortly after the Big Bang, around 13.8 billion years ago, the universe was a hot, dense soup of particles. After 380 000 years, the universe expanded and cooled down enough for the first atomic nuclei to form in a process known as Big Bang nucleosynthesis. This produced mostly hydrogen, with smaller amounts of helium and trace amounts of lithium and beryllium. Oxygen and heavier elements did not yet exist, meaning water could not yet form.

Hundreds of millions of years later, the first stars were made from clouds of hydrogen and helium. Inside these stars, nuclear fusion began to produce heavier elements. In massive stars, fusion of lighter elements created heavier elements like carbon, nitrogen, and finally oxygen (a key ingredient for water). When these massive stars reached the end of their lives, they exploded as supernovae. This scattered those elements, including oxygen, into the interstellar medium.

Now that hydrogen and oxygen existed in the universe, they began to react and form water (H₂O). This happened mainly in molecular clouds. Here, water could form in two ways. On dust grains, hydrogen and oxygen atoms stuck to the surface can react to form water ice. In hot places inside the molecular cloud like around young stars, hydrogen and oxygen gas could react to form water vapor.

As molecular clouds collapsed to form new stars, protoplanetary disks (flat disks of gas and dust moving around the star) formed around these young stars. Water in these disks could be found as water vapor or ice. This depended on how close or far away the water was from the star. The "snow line" is a place far away from the star where it is cold enough for water to freeze and turn into ice. Inside this line, water stays as a gas, but beyond it, water becomes ice. This ice allowed particles to clump together and form planets. Water got trapped in icy planetesimals, comets, and asteroids. In the inner parts of star systems, it was usually too warm for ice, so most water there was in the form of vapor. Some water may have arrived later when comets or water-rich asteroids from the colder outer regions crashed into these inner planets, bringing ice that had formed far from the star.

On some planets and moons, the conditions were just right for water to exist as a liquid, solid (ice), or gas (vapor). Earth is the best and only example we know of. Because it is the right distance from the Sun and has a protective atmosphere, it has had oceans of liquid water for billions of years. Other places, like the moons Europa, Enceladus, and Ganymede, have oceans hidden under thick layers of ice. Mars has signs that it once had rivers and lakes long ago. Comets and asteroids still hold water from the early days of the solar system.

Today, water continues to be everywhere but mostly frozen or in vapor form. It found in molecular clouds, where stars and planets are still being made. It can also be found in interstellar space as ice on dust grains. It has also been found in the atmospheres of exoplanets. At the center of galaxies, massive amounts of water, billions of times the amount on Earth has been found around black holes. But, liquid water remains extremely rare, because it requires a very narrow set of conditions. Earth is unique because it contains liquid water on its surface.

One of the biggest mysteries in astronomy is where Earth's water came from. Scientists are still trying to answer this question. Earth is special because it is the only rocky planet in our Solar System with oceans of liquid water on its surface. The other rocky planets, Mercury, Venus, and, Mars do not have large amounts of liquid water on their surface. Liquid water is important because every living thing we know needs it to survive. Earth has liquid water because it is in just the right spot in space. This spot is called the habitable zone. It is not too close to the Sun, where water would evaporate. It is also not too far away, where water would freeze. This perfect distance helps keep water in its liquid form on Earth.

There are many ideas about how Earth got its water. Most of these ideas fall into two main groups. One idea is that Earth already had the right ingredients (hydrogen and oxygen) when it formed, and those combined to make water. The other idea is that water came from space. It was carried by asteroids or comets that crashed into Earth after it formed. Some scientists think both of these ideas could be true. Earth might have gotten its water from more than one source. That makes the mystery a bit more complex, but researchers are trying their best to understand what happened in the early Solar System and how water ended up on our planet.

Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago, after the Sun was born from a huge cloud of gas and dust. The leftover material from that cloud became the rest of the Solar System, including Earth. One idea is that Earth was born with everything it needed to create oceans, lakes, and rivers. But there is a problem. The early Solar System was extremely hot, especially near the center where Earth formed. Any water on the surface would have turned into gas and escaped into space. Another idea is that Earth’s water may have come from deep inside the planet. Water might have been trapped inside rocks deep underground when Earth was forming. This water was safe from the heat because it was hidden inside minerals in Earth's mantle. Over time, volcanoes released that water as steam. When the steam cooled, it turned into rain that helped form oceans and rivers.
resumen_es: A popular science text about the properties of water, its importance for life, the economy and civilisations, its origin in the universe and the hypotheses about how it reached the Earth.

ideas_clave.idea: Water is a simple molecule whose hydrogen bonds give it unusual properties: ice floats, it stores heat, it has strong surface tension and dissolves most substances.
Every known organism depends on water, which transports substances, hosts chemical reactions in cells and regulates temperature.
Water is also central to the economy, being used mostly in agriculture but also in fishing, shipping, industry, energy production and leisure.
Access to water explains why great civilisations and cities emerged next to rivers, coasts and harbours.
Water is not exclusive to Earth: it has been detected on Mars, the Moon, icy moons, exoplanets and star-forming clouds.
Water could not exist right after the Big Bang, since oxygen was only produced later inside massive stars and spread by supernova explosions.
Water then formed in molecular clouds and, around young stars, remained as vapour or ice depending on whether it lay inside or beyond the 'snow line'.
Although water is widespread in the universe, mostly as ice or vapour, liquid water is very rare because it requires narrow conditions, and Earth is the only known case on a surface.
Earth keeps liquid water because it lies in the habitable zone, neither too close to nor too far from the Sun, yet the origin of its water remains a mystery.
Scientists debate whether Earth's water was present from its formation, possibly stored deep in its mantle and released by volcanoes, or delivered later by comets and asteroids, or both.

resumen_modelo: The text presents water as a simple compound of hydrogen and oxygen whose hydrogen bonds give it remarkable properties: it expands when it freezes, so ice floats; it absorbs heat without large temperature changes, which stabilises the climate; and it dissolves more substances than any other liquid. Water is essential to every known form of life, as it carries nutrients, hosts chemical reactions and regulates body temperature. It is equally vital for the economy, since around seventy per cent of fresh water is used in agriculture, while it also supports fishing, maritime transport, industry, hydroelectric power and leisure activities. Not surprisingly, the earliest civilisations and many major cities developed close to rivers or harbours. The second part of the text turns to the universe. Water has been detected on Mars, the Moon, several icy moons, the atmospheres of exoplanets and the clouds where stars are born. Yet it could not exist immediately after the Big Bang, because oxygen was only produced later inside massive stars and released when they exploded. Hydrogen and oxygen then combined in molecular clouds, and around young stars water remained either as vapour or as ice depending on whether it lay inside or beyond the so-called snow line; ice, in turn, helped particles clump together into planets, comets and asteroids. Consequently, although water is abundant in space, liquid water is extremely rare, and Earth, located in the habitable zone, is the only known planet with oceans on its surface. Finally, the origin of Earth's water remains unresolved: it may have been present from the start, trapped in deep rocks and released by volcanoes, or brought by comets and asteroids, or both.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Ice floats because water contracts when it freezes.
preguntas.cita: One is that it expands when it freezes. This makes ice less dense than liquid water, so ice floats.
preguntas.explicacion: Water expands (it does not contract) when it freezes; that is why ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.

preguntas.enunciado: Find in paragraph 1 a word that means “a substance able to dissolve others”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'a liquid in which other substances can be dissolved'.
preguntas.explicacion: “Solvent” is a substance that dissolves others (es: disolvente). Careful: in economics “solvent” means able to pay one’s debts (es: solvente).

preguntas.pregunta: What proportion of the human body is water, according to the text?
preguntas.cita: The human body is about 50-60% water.
preguntas.explicacion: The text gives a proportion of 50-60 %. The 70 % figure appears in the next paragraph, but it refers to the fresh water used for agriculture.

preguntas.pregunta: Which activity uses most of the fresh water consumed by people?
preguntas.cita: About 70% of the fresh water people use goes to farming.
preguntas.explicacion: Agriculture uses around 70 % of fresh water. Industry, electricity and cleaning are mentioned as uses, but their share is not given.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Singapore became wealthy partly thanks to its good harbours.
preguntas.cita: Islands with good harbors, like Singapore, also became rich and powerful because ships could stop there easily.
preguntas.explicacion: The text mentions Singapore as an example of an island that prospered thanks to its ports.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Ice has been found on Mars but not on the Moon.
preguntas.cita: Ice has been found on Mars, and even on the Moon.
preguntas.explicacion: The text states that ice has been found on Mars “and even on the Moon”, so the second part of the statement is false.

preguntas.pregunta: Why could water not form shortly after the Big Bang?
opciones: Because the universe was too cold
Because oxygen did not yet exist
respuestas: Because oxygen did not yet exist
preguntas.cita: Oxygen and heavier elements did not yet exist, meaning water could not yet form.
preguntas.explicacion: Oxygen was missing. The universe was hot, not cold; hydrogen did exist, and supernovae came much later and, in fact, scattered the oxygen.

preguntas.enunciado: Find in paragraph 7 a word for the explosion of a massive star at the end of its life (in the plural).
preguntas.pregunta: Find the word for the explosions of massive stars at the end of their lives.
preguntas.explicacion: “Supernovae” is the Latin plural of “supernova”; “supernovas” is also accepted.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the 'snow line' and why does it matter for planet formation?
respuestas: It is the distance from a young star beyond which it is cold enough for water to freeze. Beyond it, ice helped particles stick together to build planets, while inside it water remained as vapour.
preguntas.cita: The "snow line" is a place far away from the star where it is cold enough for water to freeze and turn into ice.
preguntas.explicacion: The answer must include the definition and its effect: ice helped particles to clump together and planets to form.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Mars still has rivers and lakes of liquid water on its surface.
preguntas.cita: Mars has signs that it once had rivers and lakes long ago.
preguntas.explicacion: The text speaks of evidence that Mars had rivers and lakes in the past (“once”, “long ago”), not that it has them now.

preguntas.pregunta: Why is liquid water extremely rare in the universe?
opciones: Because it requires a very narrow set of conditions
Because black holes absorb most of it
Because it only forms inside stars
respuestas: Because it requires a very narrow set of conditions
preguntas.cita: liquid water remains extremely rare, because it requires a very narrow set of conditions
preguntas.explicacion: It is rare because it requires very specific conditions. Hydrogen is abundant, huge amounts of water have been found near black holes, and water forms in molecular clouds, not inside stars.

preguntas.enunciado: Find in paragraph 12 an expression for the region around the Sun where water can stay liquid.
preguntas.pregunta: Find the expression for the region around a star where water can stay liquid.
preguntas.cita: This spot is called the habitable zone.
preguntas.explicacion: The “habitable zone” (es: zona de habitabilidad) is neither so close to the star that water evaporates nor so far away that it freezes.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Most scientists now agree that comets brought more water to Earth than asteroids did.
preguntas.explicacion: The text mentions comets and asteroids as possible sources, but it does not compare their contribution or talk about a scientific consensus.

preguntas.pregunta: What problem does the idea that Earth was born with its water face, and how might it be solved?
respuestas: The early Solar System was so hot near Earth that surface water would have evaporated into space. However, water may have survived trapped in minerals deep in the mantle and later been released by volcanoes as steam, which became rain.
preguntas.cita: Any water on the surface would have turned into gas and escaped into space.
preguntas.explicacion: You need to explain the objection (the heat of the early solar system) and the possible solution (water trapped in the mantle and released by volcanic activity).

preguntas.pregunta: According to the text, why did access to water influence where civilisations developed?
respuestas: Because rivers and coasts provided water for living and farming and made trade and travel easier, so having water could turn a small village into a powerful civilisation.
preguntas.cita: Being close to rivers or oceans made it easier to trade and travel.
preguntas.explicacion: This is a synthesis question on paragraph 4: water made life, trade and travel easier, which favoured the development of cities and civilisations.
